blocks.text: A student team holds a single two-hour 'design review' the week before their parts are due at the workshop. The presenter talks for 110 minutes, nobody writes anything down, and three weeks later two people remember an agreement to enlarge a bearing seat and the others remember the opposite. A review that does not produce a written list of actions with owners and dates has not found problems; it has only talked about them.

blocks.markdown: A **design review** is a planned meeting at which people other than the designers examine the design against its requirements and decide whether the project may proceed. Its value comes from fresh eyes, an agreed objective, a recorded outcome and follow-up. Reviews occur at fixed stages, because what can usefully be judged depends on how much of the design exists.

rows: Do the requirements make sense, and is the chosen concept viable and better than the alternatives?
Requirements list, concept sketches, decision matrix, risks
After architecture and sizing, before detailed drawings
Does the design meet requirements in principle, with interfaces and key risks under control?
Layout, sizing calculations, interface definitions, budgets, test plan outline
When the detailed design is complete
Is the design complete and correct enough to release for manufacture?
Full drawings, detailed calculations, tolerance and safety analyses, test plan, risk closure
blocks.caption: Three common design review types (names and stages vary between organisations).

blocks.markdown: **Roles.** The **chair** controls the agenda and time and ensures decisions are made. The **presenter** (the design team) explains the design and the evidence. **Reviewers** are independent people with the skills to challenge it (a stress engineer, a manufacturing engineer, a safety adviser). The **recorder** writes down every finding and decision as it happens. Actions are assigned to named **owners**. The reviewer's task is to test the design, not to redesign it in the meeting.

blocks.title: A well-formed review action
blocks.text: Each finding is recorded as an action containing: a unique number; a precise description of the problem and the required response; the **owner** (one named person); the **severity** (for example critical, major, minor, defined in advance); the **due date**; and a status (open, closed, verified). Critical actions are normally closed before the project passes the review, major ones by an agreed date, and minor ones can be tracked more loosely.

blocks.title: Recording findings as actions
blocks.prompt: During a PDR the reviewers note that the key in a drive shaft was checked only for shear and not for bearing (crushing) stress, that the gearbox mass is 0.4 kg over budget, and that the drawing title block is missing the revision. Write these as actions with severity.

steps.text: Finding 1: key bearing stress not checked. Severity: major (a possible structural failure mode is unassessed). Action: calculate bearing stress and compare with allowable stress. Owner: drive lead. Due: before CDR.

Finding 2: mass 0.4 kg over budget. Severity: major (breaches a constraint requirement). Action: identify a mass reduction of at least 0.4 kg or request a change to the limit. Owner: project engineer. Due: within 14 days.
Finding 3: missing revision on drawing. Severity: minor (documentation). Action: correct title block. Owner: draftsperson. Due: next issue.
Check each action: one owner, a clear closure condition, a severity, a date. 'Look into the key' would not be acceptable.

blocks.answer: Three actions recorded with owner, severity and due date; the two major ones must be closed before the project is cleared to proceed.

blocks.markdown: **Evaluating against a checklist.** To keep reviews consistent, reviewers work through a checklist of questions (requirements traced? loads and assumptions stated? calculations checked? tolerances and fits specified? manufacturing and assembly considered? safety hazards controlled? test plan present?). Each item receives one of three ratings: **pass** (the evidence is adequate), **concern** (evidence is incomplete, assumed or marginal, and an action is needed but the design is not clearly wrong) or **fail** (the requirement is not met, or the evidence is missing for a critical item). Every concern and fail must produce an action.

blocks.caption: One common way to summarise a checklist. w_i is the weight of item i (larger for safety-critical items). The score informs the discussion; a single fail on a critical item can still block approval.

blocks.title: Scoring a checklist
blocks.prompt: Five equally weighted items are rated: pass, pass, pass, concern, fail. Find the score and say what the review should do.

steps.text: Decision: the failed item needs a corrective action and re-review; the concern needs an action; the review cannot be passed with an open fail on a critical item regardless of the 70% score.

blocks.answer: Score 70%; actions are required for the concern and the fail, and the review is conditional on closing them.

items: Agree the review objective, the type of review and the pass criteria in advance.
Circulate the review pack early so reviewers can prepare.
Record every finding live, with owner, severity and due date.
Rate checklist items pass, concern or fail and raise actions for the last two.
Track actions to closure and verify them, then report the review outcome.

blocks.title: The outcome is a decision
blocks.text: Each review ends with a stated decision: proceed, proceed with actions, or repeat the review. Recording the decision and its conditions is as important as recording the findings.

blocks.title: Do not redesign in the room
blocks.text: Reviewers who start solving the problem consume the time needed to find other problems. Record the finding, name an owner and move on; the designer solves it afterwards.

points: Concept, preliminary and critical reviews ask progressively more detailed questions: viability of concept, feasibility of architecture, then readiness for manufacture.
Every finding is recorded as an action with a named owner, severity and due date, and tracked to closure.
Checklist items are rated pass, concern or fail, and every concern or fail generates an action.

questions.stem: What is the primary objective of a critical design review (CDR)?

options.text: To confirm that the detailed design is complete and correct enough to release for manufacture
To decide between several competing concept ideas
To collect the customer's first statement of needs
To set the project schedule for the first time

questions.correctOptionText: To confirm that the detailed design is complete and correct enough to release for manufacture

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CDR comes at the end of detailed design and gates release.
distractorRationale.b: Concept choice belongs to the concept review.
distractorRationale.c: Capturing needs happens at the start, before concepts are reviewed.
distractorRationale.d: Scheduling is a planning activity, not the aim of the review.

questions.explanation: The later the review, the more detailed the questions. The critical review checks drawings, calculations and test plans for readiness to manufacture.

questions.stem: At a concept design review, which question is most appropriate?

options.text: Are the requirements sensible, and is the chosen concept viable and better than the rejected alternatives?
Is every dimension on the drawings toleranced correctly?
Have all the fasteners been torque-checked on the prototype?
Is the final test report complete?

questions.correctOptionText: Are the requirements sensible, and is the chosen concept viable and better than the rejected alternatives?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is what can be judged when only requirements and concepts exist.
distractorRationale.b: Drawings are not yet complete at this stage.
distractorRationale.c: No prototype exists at the concept stage.

questions.explanation: The review must ask what can be judged at the time. At concept stage that is the soundness of requirements and the reasoning behind the concept choice.

questions.stem: A team has completed sizing calculations, a layout drawing with defined interfaces, a mass budget and an outline test plan. Detailed drawings are not started. Which review fits this stage?

options.text: A preliminary design review
A critical design review
A concept design review
A post-test review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the architecture and sizing exist but detail does not.
distractorRationale.b: The critical review requires complete detailed design.
distractorRationale.c: The concept review comes before sizing and layout.

questions.explanation: A preliminary review tests feasibility and the control of key risks once the architecture and sizing are defined. It happens before the effort of detailed drawings is committed.

questions.stem: Which of these is a well-formed review action?

options.text: 'Recalculate the bearing life with a 1.5 times load factor. Owner: S. Okafor. Severity: major. Due: 14 June.'
'Look into the bearings.'
'The team should think about loads.'
'Somebody to check this soon.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'Recalculate the bearing life with a 1.5 times load factor. Owner: S. Okafor. Severity: major. Due: 14 June.'

distractorRationale.a: Correct: specific, with owner, severity and due date.
distractorRationale.b: No owner, severity, date or closure condition.
distractorRationale.c: Vague, with no owner or date.
distractorRationale.d: No named owner and no date.

questions.explanation: An action must say what is to be done, by whom, how urgent it is and by when. Otherwise it cannot be tracked or closed.

questions.stem: During a checklist review a hand calculation for a shaft exists, but it uses a load estimate that has not been confirmed by the customer. How should the item be rated?

options.text: Concern, with an action to confirm the load and update the calculation
Pass, because a calculation exists
Fail, because the load is uncertain so the shaft is unsafe
Not rated, because uncertain items are ignored

questions.correctOptionText: Concern, with an action to confirm the load and update the calculation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: evidence exists but is incomplete or assumption-based, so an action is needed.
distractorRationale.b: A calculation based on an unconfirmed input is not fully adequate evidence.
distractorRationale.c: Nothing shows the shaft is unsafe; the evidence is incomplete, not negative.
distractorRationale.d: All items must be rated and actions raised for those below pass.

questions.explanation: A concern marks evidence that is marginal or depends on an unverified assumption. A fail is for an unmet requirement or missing critical evidence.

questions.stem: A checklist has 25 items. 17 are rated pass, 6 are rated concern and 2 are rated fail. What percentage of the items are rated pass?
questions.explanation: The percentage is $17/25\times100=68\%$. The remaining 8 items each need an action, and the two fails may block approval.

questions.stem: A review raises 22 actions: 4 critical, 9 major and 9 minor. The review rules require every critical and major action to be closed before release. What percentage of the actions must be closed before release?
questions.explanation: Critical plus major is $4+9=13$ actions, and $13/22\times100=59.1\%$. The minor actions may be closed after release by the agreed date.

questions.stem: Three safety-critical checklist items have weight 3 each and are rated pass, concern and fail. Four other items have weight 1 each and are rated pass, pass, pass and concern. Using ratings pass 1, concern 0.5, fail 0, what is the weighted score as a percentage of the maximum?
questions.explanation: The weighted sum for the safety items is $3(1+0.5+0)=4.5$ and for the others $1+1+1+0.5=3.5$, giving 8.0. The maximum is $3\times3+4\times1=13$, so the score is $8/13=61.5\%$.

questions.stem: Explain how concept, preliminary and critical design reviews differ in objective and in the evidence expected, and say why holding only a single review at the end of a project is risky.
markingGuide: Concept review: requirements and concept viability, with concept sketches and the decision matrix
Preliminary review: architecture, sizing, interfaces and key risks, before detailed drawings
Critical review: complete detailed design, drawings, calculations and test plan, with approval to release for manufacture
Risk of a single late review: problems found when changes are costly or impossible
Early reviews gate the spend and let corrections be cheap
questions.explanation: Each review is a gate that asks only what can be judged at that stage. A single late review finds fundamental errors only after drawings and parts have been made.

questions.stem: A reviewer finds that a gearbox design has a tolerance stack that was not analysed (critical for gear mesh), that the bill of materials has two typing errors, and that the lubrication method is described only as 'to be decided'. Rate each item pass, concern or fail with reasons, and write the corresponding action entries including owner, severity and due date.
markingGuide: Tolerance stack not analysed on a critical item: fail (or concern if analysis is promised), severity major or critical
BOM typing errors: pass or minor concern with minor severity
Lubrication undecided: concern or fail depending on the requirement, with severity major
Each action has a specific description of closure condition
Each action has a named owner role and a due date tied to the next review
Justification of ratings by evidence available
questions.explanation: Ratings depend on the evidence for each item. Every concern or fail generates an action with a single owner, a severity and a date.
